children: 1111 GMT - A more risk-averse market has lifted the dollar only modestly as a safe-haven asset, Societe Generale's Kit Juckes says in a note. The realization that the Middle conflict is likely to drag on, together with higher energy costs, hasn't managed to lift the DXY dollar index back above 100 after its decline to 98 over the summer, he says. "This is partly due to increased optimism about the growth outlook elsewhere, relative to the concerns that prevailed at the start of the conflict," Juckes says. The DXY last trades up 0.1% at 99.671. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1043 GMT - Developed market sovereign bond yields are close to multi-year highs, making them increasingly more appealing than their corporate bond peers, Societe Generale's Juan Valencia says in a note. Sovereign bonds are perceived as safer assets compared to corporate bonds, as the latter face a higher risk of getting a rating downgrade or defaulting when bond yields are high, Valencia says. Elevated government bond yields could spark a migration from corporate bonds to government bonds, he says. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

1034 GMT - Sterling remains in a difficult position as the Bank of England contends with elevated inflation and tepid U.K. economic growth, Marex's Jonathan Pryor says in a note. "Growth is still underwhelming, and unless we pin our hopes on some sort of productivity increase from AI, which is still in extremely early days, there doesn't seem to be a factor that's going to get the U.K. economy out of the woods," he says. At the same time, inflation is still uncomfortably high and energy prices continue to rise, he says. Given these factors and high U.K. government bond yields, the BOE has a challenging job, he says. Sterling trades steady at $1.3472. The euro rises 0.1% to 0.8566 pounds.(renae.dyer@wsj.com)

1002 GMT - Credit markets face growing threats from high sovereign bond yields, AI disruption concerns and geopolitical worries, which could cause credit spreads to widen, Societe Generale's Juan Valencia says in a note. U.S. dollar and euro credit spreads have remained fairly resilient due to strong demand for the assets, despite the volatility in stocks and sovereign bonds in recent months. A new shock could trigger sharp and sustained credit spread widening, however, Valencia says. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0953 GMT - U.S. Treasury yields and the dollar are steady in mid-morning European trade ahead of the Federal Reserve's decision, when a rate increase is widely expected. A 25-basis-point rate rise is near certain given market pricing of an over 90% probability of this outcome, according to LSEG data. Attention will focus on the voting split, particularly Chairman Kevin Warsh's stance, DHF Capital S.A's Bas Kooijman says in a note. "A hawkish message signalling further increases could push yields higher and support the dollar, while any attempt to downplay the prospect of additional tightening could add volatility to bond and currency markets," he says. The 10-year Treasury yields are steady at 4.994%, according to Tradeweb. The DXY index trades at 99.642. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0941 GMT - The dollar might struggle to rise unless the Federal Reserve cements expectations for an extended interest-rate rise cycle in a decision later, MUFG Bank's Lee Hardman says in a note. The market is nearly fully pricing a 25 basis-point rate rise Wednesday and almost 95 basis points of tightening by September 2027, LSEG data show. This pricing creates a high bar for the Fed to sound more "hawkish" in favor of raising rates than expected, Hardman says. The Fed's communication is unlikely to provide a clear signal over how much further tightening is likely to be needed, he says. The decision is at 1800 GMT. The DXY dollar index trades flat at 99.639. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0937 GMT - Investors' attention is on the U.S. Federal Reserve interest-rate decision due at 1800 GMT, where a rate increase is widely expected. However, traders will also pay attention to the Fed's communication and policymakers' commitment to tackling inflation over the coming months, Tickmill Group's Patrick Munnelly says in a note. "The broader reaction will be clearest in the dollar, gold and equities, where investors will quickly signal whether they see the Fed as regaining control or simply chasing a market that has already moved ahead of it," he says. Ten-year U.S. Treasurys rare last steady at 4.996%, having hit a 19-year high of 5.041% this week, LSEG data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0927 GMT - The euro could fall slightly against the dollar if the Federal Reserve raises interest rates and signals further possible tightening in a decision later, ING's Francesco Pesole says in a note. Looking further ahead, the Fed and European Central Bank are unlikely to deliver another rate rise, implying room for money markets to significantly reduce pricing of additional U.S. and eurozone rate increases, he says. This would limit the scope for the euro to fall. "A coordinated move lower in front-end rates can put a floor under euro-dollar, as would likely happen alongside a decline in energy prices." The euro trades flat at $1.1539 and ING expects it to reach $1.15 after the Fed decision at 1800 GMT. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0921 GMT - Weak credit transmission, prolonged property correction and subdued private demand are likely to prevent a meaningful recovery and constrain growth into 2027 for China, Julius Baer economist Sophie Altermatt writes in a note. China's economy remained highly uneven in August as stronger industrial production and robust exports contrasted with further weakness in consumption, investment and property activity, she adds. Weakening credit dynamics confirm a weak appetite for loans among households and businesses, she says. There will likely be faster fiscal execution to help stabilize growth toward year end, but not to generate a broad-based recovery, Julius Baer says. The bank maintains its 2026 GDP growth forecast at 4.5%, the low end of the official target range.(jiahui.huang@wsj.com; @ivy_jiahuihuang)

0916 GMT - The cost of insuring euro-denominated credit against default falls slightly as global markets sentiment stabilizes. Global stocks and government bonds trim the losses posted on Monday and Tuesday as focus is on the U.S. Federal Reserve interest-rate decision due at 1800 GMT. Investors widely expect the Fed to raise interest rates by a quarter point. Attention will also be on the Fed communication and any signals on potential interest-rate rises at future meetings. The iTraxx Europe Crossover index of euro high-yield credit default swaps falls 2 basis points to 263bps, S&P Global Market Intelligence data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0913 GMT - China's tepid GDP growth in August raises the probability of additional fiscal stimulus in 4Q, BNP Paribas economists say in a note. Based on the bank's estimates, real GDP growth last month was 4.3% on year. Policymakers may introduce new fiscal stimulus in October if 3Q growth slows to around 4.0% and if the economy fails to recover despite having support from fiscal measures. Economists say fresh stimulus measures may include more policy-based financial instruments, as fiscal policy is the most effective lever to counter short-term weak growth. (amanda.lee@wsj.com)

0911 GMT - Sterling could fall further against the euro as the latest U.K. inflation data might tilt the Bank of England towards dampening elevated interest-rate rise expectations in a decision Thursday, ING's Francesco Pesole says in a note. Data Wednesday showed inflation accelerated to 3.1% in August, as expected, but core and services inflation were unchanged. That supports the case for the BOE to sound cautious about raising rates, he says. "We still target a return above 0.8600 in euro/sterling in the coming days." The euro rises 0.1% to 0.8570 pounds. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

title: Risk Aversion Fails to Provide Much Support to Dollar — Market Talk
